Nov 18, 2026

Cloud Connector is now generally available

Rules

Cloud Connector is now generally available to all customers.

Cloud Connector lets you route matching requests to public object storage in Cloudflare R2, Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Microsoft Azure Blob Storage, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Object Storage. You can create and manage routing rules in the Cloudflare dashboard, using Rules expressions to control which requests are sent to each provider.

Refer to the Cloud Connector documentation to get started.

Nov 17, 2026

Configure a separate WAN gateway for each appliance in a high availability site

Cloudflare One ApplianceCloudflare OneCloudflare WAN

You can now give each Cloudflare One Appliance in a high availability (HA) site its own default gateway on a static WAN. Before this change, both appliances in an HA pair shared the same WAN gateway. Now each appliance can connect to its own Internet circuit, such as a different ISP for each appliance, with its own static IP and gateway.

  • In the dashboard, when you configure a static WAN on an HA site, enter the secondary appliance's gateway in the new Secondary gateway address field, next to Primary gateway address.
  • In the API, set static_addressing.secondary_gateway_address when you create or update a WAN. To remove the value with a PATCH request, set it to null.

The field is optional. If you leave it blank, the secondary appliance uses the primary gateway address, which matches how HA sites worked before. You can only use this field on sites in HA mode.

For details, refer to About high availability configurations.

Nov 12, 2026

New hash functions — sha1(), md5(), and sha512()

Rules

Cloudflare Rules supports three new hash functions: sha1(), md5(), and sha512(). Use them to compute hashes for systems that require these algorithms.

Like the existing sha256() function, each accepts a string or byte array and returns raw bytes:

Function Algorithm Output length
md5() MD5 16 bytes
sha1() SHA-1 20 bytes
sha512() SHA-512 64 bytes

For details, refer to the sha1(), md5(), and sha512() function references.

Nov 12, 2026

Cloudflare Tunnel extends URL normalization

Cloudflare TunnelCloudflare Tunnel for SASE

Starting from version 2026.11.0, Cloudflare Tunnel extends the URL normalization introduced in 2026.10.0. Normalization now handles semicolon-delimited path parameters before matching ingress rules. This improves security for tunnels with rules that require Cloudflare Access validation. The URL path sent to your origin stays the same.

Starting 2027-02-08, new cloudflared releases will turn on URL normalization by default. This replaces the previously announced date of 2027-01-25, giving you time to test the updated behavior. Upgrade to version 2026.11.0 or later and test your path-based routing before that date, including rules that match paths containing semicolons. Configurations without rules requiring Access validation are unaffected.

This setting is currently off by default. To turn it on, run:

Alternatively, set TUNNEL_DISABLE_PATH_NORMALIZATION=false on each cloudflared replica and restart it.

For more information, refer to ingress matching and Access validation at the origin.

Nov 4, 2026

New managed rule to help mitigate CVE-2026-98432.

Cloudflare Network Firewall

Cloudflare Network Firewall has a new managed rule to help mitigate the Linux IPv4 TCP use-after-free vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432 ↗︎):

  • Rule name: Block CVE-2026-98432 ↗︎ traffic
  • Rule ID: 6a4df2bf984946a88c74b07349557e83

The rule is disabled by default. To use it:

  1. Go to Networking > Firewall Policies > Managed Rulesets.
  2. Enable the rule with action Log first.
  3. Review traffic that matches the rule.
  4. If the matching traffic is not expected for your environment, change the action to Block.

For more information on enabling managed rulesets, refer to Enable managed rulesets.

For more details about the vulnerability, including an agent assessment prompt and evidence sources, refer to the Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire briefing ↗︎.

Nov 4, 2026

Steer Cloudflare One users and private networks to the same endpoint with session affinity and hash steering in private load balancers

Load BalancingCloudflare TunnelCloudflare Mesh

Private load balancers can now keep each user on the same endpoint. This helps with applications that keep session state on a single server.

Two options are available:

  • Hash endpoint steering. In the dashboard, set a pool's Endpoint steering to Hash. Each user is mapped to an endpoint within the pool.
  • Session affinity. With the API, set session_affinity to ip_cookie on the load balancer. Each user stays on the same endpoint while it remains healthy and your pools do not change. Refer to Session affinity.

For traffic from the Cloudflare One Client, Cloudflare identifies the user by their device, so a user stays on the same endpoint even if their IP address changes. For other traffic, such as from a Cloudflare WAN site, Cloudflare uses the source IP address.

This works for endpoints reached through Cloudflare Tunnel, Cloudflare Mesh, and Cloudflare WAN. Affinity pins the endpoint, not the cloudflared or Mesh replica that carries the traffic.

To learn how private load balancing fits with your connectors, refer to Load balance private network traffic.

Oct 30, 2026

Cloudflare WAN supports regional Gateway HTTP inspection

Data Localization SuiteCloudflare WANCloudflare One

Cloudflare WAN traffic can now use a Gateway processing region with Regional Services. HTTPS traffic enters a Cloudflare data center (that may be outside the selected region) via an IPsec or GRE tunnel, or through Direct CNI, and remains encrypted until Gateway forwards it to the selected region for TLS decryption and HTTP inspection. This feature gives organizations control over where their sensitive traffic is processed, supporting their data sovereignty goals.

This feature requires unified routing. The processing region applies to Gateway HTTP traffic and does not apply to Gateway DNS or network policy processing.

Contact your account team to configure a processing region. For supported regions, configuration details, and limitations, refer to Data residency for Cloudflare One.

Oct 30, 2026

Workers subrequests now preserve context for BYOIP destinations

WorkersBYOIPBots

Cloudflare now preserves Workers context when a subrequest targets a Cloudflare-proxied hostname using Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP). These requests are identified as Cloudflare-to-Cloudflare traffic instead of external Internet traffic.

Previously, some BYOIP subrequests could lose Workers context and original client signals. This could cause security rules to behave unexpectedly, Bot Management to evaluate an internal Cloudflare connection instead of the original client, or affected requests to return false 403 responses.

Workers subrequests to BYOIP destinations now preserve the CF-Worker header and cf.worker.upstream_zone field. This supports consistent security rule evaluation across same-zone and cross-zone subrequests.

Bot Management fields on the destination zone now represent the original end-user connection for affected BYOIP subrequests. Bot scores, verified bot status, and JA3/JA4 fingerprints no longer represent the internal connection between Cloudflare services.

Because Cloudflare-proxied BYOIP destinations now follow standard Workers subrequest handling, cross-zone requests set CF-Connecting-IP to the Workers client IP address 2a06:98c0:3600::103 for security reasons. This applies when a Worker in one Cloudflare zone sends a subrequest to a hostname in another Cloudflare zone. Same-zone subrequests continue to reflect the client IP through CF-Connecting-IP.

For more information, refer to Cloudflare BYOIP, Workers subrequests, and CF-Connecting-IP in Worker subrequests.

Oct 29, 2026

View your data localization settings in one dashboard page

Data Localization SuiteSSL/TLS

The Cloudflare dashboard now includes a Data Localization Suite Overview, a read-only view of the data localization settings on your account. It shows your Regional Services, Customer Metadata Boundary, and Geo Key Manager settings in one place, so you no longer need to check several dashboard pages and APIs to see where your traffic is processed and where your logs and private keys are stored.

To find it, go to Application Security > Data Localization Suite, or search for "DLS" in the dashboard.

The Overview has a tab for each product:

  • Regional Services: regionalized hostnames (filter by region or zone), regionalized IP bindings, and regionalized Spectrum applications, each with its region.
  • Customer Metadata Boundary: whether the boundary is on, the region (US or EU), and whether out-of-region access is allowed.
  • Geo Key Manager: every custom certificate with a geo policy, with its hostname, zone, region, and status.

Each item links to the dashboard page where you change its setting, and each tab links to the product's documentation.

To learn more, refer to the Data Localization Suite documentation.

Oct 22, 2026

Cloudflare Tunnel supports URL normalization

Cloudflare TunnelCloudflare Tunnel for SASE

Starting from version 2026.10.0, Cloudflare Tunnel can normalize URLs before matching ingress rules. This improves security for tunnels with rules that require Cloudflare Access validation. The URL path sent to your origin stays the same.

In three months, starting 2027-01-25, new cloudflared releases will turn on URL normalization by default. Test your path-based routing before that date, as this change may affect which ingress rule matches a request. Configurations without rules requiring Access validation are unaffected.

This setting is currently off by default. To turn it on, run:

Alternatively, set TUNNEL_DISABLE_PATH_NORMALIZATION=false on each cloudflared replica and restart it.

For more information, refer to ingress matching and Access validation at the origin.

Oct 22, 2026

Granular Tunnel Read And Monitor role is generally available

Cloudflare FundamentalsCloudflare OneCloudflare Tunnel for SASECloudflare Tunnel

The Cloudflare Tunnel - Granular Connector cloudflared Read And Monitor role is now generally available. You can grant a member read access and log streaming for specific Cloudflare Tunnel instances without granting write access or access to every Tunnel in your account.

This role includes the same access as Cloudflare Tunnel - Granular Connector cloudflared Read: viewing selected Tunnels, their IP and hostname routes, and connector host details. It also grants remote log streaming, so support operators can troubleshoot a Tunnel without changing its configuration. The existing Read role does not grant log streaming access.

To assign the role, follow Grant a granular permission. For the available roles, refer to the resource-scoped roles reference.

Oct 16, 2026

50,000 routes per account and Tunnels for Platforms

Cloudflare TunnelCloudflare Tunnel for SASECloudflare MeshCloudflare One

Two changes make it easier to run Cloudflare Tunnel at scale.

50,000 routes per account by default

The default limit for routes is now 50,000 per account, up from 1,000. This limit covers CIDR routes and hostname routes for Cloudflare Tunnel and Cloudflare Mesh. The new limit applies to every account automatically, with no action required.

Published applications (public hostnames) are not routes and are not affected by this limit. Each tunnel supports roughly 5,000–10,000 published applications, depending on the size of its configuration. For details, refer to Published application limits.

Tunnels for Platforms

Every account includes 1,000 tunnels. With Tunnels for Platforms, you can now run more than 1,000 tunnels in a single account — for example, one tunnel per device, per end customer, or per development environment.

To buy additional tunnels, go to Networking > Tunnels and select Buy more tunnels in the Usage card. Additional tunnels are billed at $4.50 per tunnel per month. Enterprise customers can contact their account team for committed or usage-based pricing.

Go to Tunnels ↗

For pricing, limits, and best practices for managing large tunnel fleets, refer to Tunnels for Platforms.

Oct 15, 2026

BGP route filtering for IPsec and GRE tunnels

Cloudflare WANMagic TransitCloudflare One

Cloudflare WAN and Magic Transit IPsec and GRE tunnels now support BGP import and export filtering.

Create reusable filter profiles that specify an allow or deny action and a list of Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) targets with exact, more-specific, or prefix-length matching. Each tunnel supports one import filter and one export filter.

You can create and assign profiles through the dashboard, API, or Terraform. Profile changes apply without resetting the BGP session.

For configuration details, refer to:

  • Filter BGP routes for Cloudflare WAN
  • Filter BGP routes for Magic Transit
Oct 14, 2026

Remove surrounding bytes with trim functions

Rules

Cloudflare Rules supports three new functions for removing surrounding bytes. Use them to remove whitespace before comparing request values. All HTTP products support these functions on all plans:

  • trim() removes bytes from both ends.
  • trim_start() removes bytes from the start.
  • trim_end() removes bytes from the end.

By default, these functions remove ASCII whitespace. An optional constant string specifies a custom set of bytes.

If the input value is nil, these functions return nil.

Oct 9, 2026

Failed detections field available in Rules

WAFRules

You can now use cf.appsec.request.failed_detections to control how your rules handle requests when a security detection reports a failure.

The field is an Array<String> of detection IDs that reports failures from content scanning, WAF attack score, attack signature detection, leaked credentials detection, and AI prompt detections for personally identifiable information (PII), prompt injection, custom topics, and unsafe topics.

The field does not alter the existing behavior of detections. Use it in rules to choose how to handle requests with reported failures.

When no failures are reported, the field returns []. You can use it on all plans, but your plan must still include the detections and rule features you want to use.

Supported rules:

  • Custom rules at the zone and account levels
  • Rate limiting rules at the zone and account levels
  • Request Header Transform Rules at the zone level

For more information, refer to the Failed detections field reference.

Oct 5, 2026

BGP over IPsec and GRE tunnels generally available

Cloudflare WANMagic TransitCloudflare One

BGP peering over IPsec and GRE tunnels is generally available for Cloudflare WAN and Magic Transit. You can use it for production workloads.

BGP peering exchanges routes dynamically between your devices and your Cloudflare virtual network routing table. You no longer need to update static routes manually as your network changes.

BGP over IPsec and GRE tunnels is available to all accounts that use Unified Routing. No enablement is required. BGP over CNI remains in closed beta.

For configuration details, refer to:

  • Configure BGP routes for Cloudflare WAN
  • Configure BGP routes for Magic Transit

Use cf.random_seed to select approximately 10% of requests at random:

Oct 2, 2026

Protect Quick Tunnels with email authentication

Cloudflare Tunnel

You can now restrict who can access a Quick Tunnel. Use the new --allowed-mail flag in cloudflared to require visitors to authenticate with a one-time PIN sent to their email before they reach your local service.

Previously, anyone with a trycloudflare.com URL could access the service behind it. Protected Quick Tunnels let you share a local development server, webhook receiver, or demo with specific people without creating a Cloudflare account or configuring a domain.

You can allow:

  • A single email address: --allowed-mail alice@example.com
  • Multiple email addresses, by repeating the flag or using a comma-separated list: --allowed-mail 'alice@example.com,bob@example.com'
  • Every address on a domain: --allowed-mail '*@example.com'

Visitors do not need a Cloudflare account. Access ends for everyone when you stop the cloudflared process.

To get started, update cloudflared to the latest version and refer to Restrict access by email.

Sep 30, 2026

Longer rule descriptions in logs

Rules

Cloudflare logs now include up to 128 bytes of a rule description, increased from 80 bytes. Longer descriptions provide more context when investigating matched rules and make it easier to identify the relevant rule without referring back to its configuration.

Descriptions longer than 128 bytes are truncated without splitting a UTF-8 character. This change does not affect the Rulesets API, which continues to accept rule descriptions of up to 4,096 bytes.

For more information, refer to Rule object structure and properties.

Sep 29, 2026

Identify Mesh, Workers VPC, and Cloudflare Tunnel replicas in network logs

Cloudflare MeshCloudflare TunnelCloudflare OneGatewayWorkers VPC

You can now tell a person on a laptop apart from a Mesh node or an AI agent running on Workers, without matching on connector email addresses or Mesh IP ranges — and see exactly which Cloudflare Tunnel and cloudflared replica received each session.

Gateway network logs and Zero Trust Network Session Logs now identify two new kinds of traffic:

  • Mesh — Traffic sent from or delivered to a Cloudflare Mesh node. Previously, Mesh nodes were logged the same way as devices running the Cloudflare One Client, because Mesh nodes run the client in headless mode.
  • Workers VPC — Traffic sent by a Worker through a Workers VPC binding. Previously, Workers VPC sessions were not recorded in Network Session Logs.

Gateway network logs

To view these values in the dashboard, go to Zero Trust > Insights & Logs > Logs > Network logs, select Columns, and turn on Traffic Source and Traffic Destination. Both values also appear under Network query details when you open a log entry.

Network Session Logs

The zero_trust_network_sessions dataset, available through Logpush, includes the following fields:

Field Description
OnrampType How the session entered Cloudflare One. Values: CF1_CLIENT, MESH, WORKERS_VPC, MAGIC, OTHER.
Offramp Where the session was routed. Sessions routed to a Mesh node report MESH.
SourceName Name of the Worker that started the session. Only populated for Workers VPC sessions.
SourceID Stable identifier of the Worker that started the session. Only populated for Workers VPC sessions.
DestinationReplicaID The replica that served the session, such as a specific replica of a Mesh node or a cloudflared replica of a Cloudflare Tunnel.

For example, OnrampType = 'WORKERS_VPC' AND Offramp = 'MESH' returns every session where a Worker reached a service behind a Mesh node, and SourceName tells you which Worker it was.

Redeploy your Workers

SourceName and SourceID are only populated for Workers deployed after 29 September 2026. To include them for an existing Worker, redeploy it — for example, with npx wrangler deploy. No code changes are required.

See which tunnel and replica received a session

With DestinationReplicaID, you can now confirm which Cloudflare Tunnel and which cloudflared replica received traffic for a specific session. Combine it with the existing DestinationTunnelID field to trace a session to an exact tunnel replica — or Mesh node replica — when you run multiple replicas for high availability. The replica ID matches the Connector ID shown in the dashboard, so you can stream that replica's logs with cloudflared tail --connector-id.

Sessions logged before this change are not backfilled. For all available fields, refer to Zero Trust Network Session Logs.
